implementation_notes: Redux Toolkit is the sanctioned way to write Redux today: configureStore builds the store with the standard middleware and devtools wiring, createSlice generates action creators and reducers from a name plus reducer functions (running them through Immer so reducers may 'mutate' a draft safely), and react-redux's useSelector/useDispatch connect components. The dispatcher of classic Flux is folded into the store, so a separate dispatcher or several stores are no longer needed, and async work goes into createAsyncThunk or a listener middleware. What replaces the classic structure is the toolkit's slice API; hand-written reducers only remain justified where the store is tiny or the dependency is unacceptable.
pitfalls: Immer makes the draft mutable, so both mutating the draft and returning a value in the same createSlice reducer throws - pick one style per reducer.
Immer only tracks plain objects/arrays inside the slice; class instances, Maps and Sets need manual copies that the draft does not see.
A selector that builds a new object each call (useSelector(s => ({ a: s.a, b: s.b }))) re-renders on every dispatch; select single fields or pass shallowEqual.
Importing the singleton store everywhere makes tests share state; export a makeStore() factory too and keep the default export for the app entry only.

variants.name: React useReducer + Context as the store
variants.idiom_name: useReducer + context provider (framework built-ins, no dependency)
variants.implementation_notes: React's built-in useReducer is a reducer-and-dispatch pair: the reducer is a pure (state, action) => state function, dispatch is the only way to update, and a context provider publishes the resulting state and dispatch to consumers - a minimal Redux with no dependency and a subtree scope instead of an application-wide one. It fits mid-size trees and single features, and it is what the Redux docs recommend trying before reaching for Redux. The trade-offs against Redux Toolkit are real: every context consumer re-renders on each change, there is no middleware, devtools or time travel, and two providers create two independent states.
pitfalls: Every context consumer re-renders when the provider value changes; split state and dispatch into separate contexts so dispatch-only children stay still.
The context value object is new on every render unless memoised, which makes the provider cascade to every consumer even when the state is unchanged.
React StrictMode double-invokes reducers in development, so a reducer with a side effect or a non-idempotent mutation corrupts state on the second call.
A provider is a subtree store, not a global one: nesting two providers silently creates two states and breaks the single-source-of-truth promise.
